Meta surged 12% in a month after launching Muse Wonder and Mark Zuckerberg pledging to maintain AI capital spending at scale.

Meta's 12% monthly gain dwarfs Microsoft's 7% rise and Alphabet's near-flat 0.3%, leaving Meta far ahead of megacap peers.

Ad revenue alone funds Meta's entire AI budget, making engagement growth and ad pricing the decisive levers for any payoff.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Meta didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat META. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stock has pulled well ahead of its megacap peers on the strength of its newest artificial intelligence (AI) model. Shares of Meta Platforms are up 0.6% in afternoon trading, extending a 12% climb over the past month that has carried Meta Platforms stock to $742.11.

Fritz Jorgensen / iStock Editorial via Getty Images
META Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

That run leaves holders of Meta Platforms stock with a classic dilemma. Locking in profits protects gains already on the books, while holding on keeps their money working if the AI push delivers more. The right answer depends on how much of the AI story each holder wants to own at this price.

Muse Wonder and a Spending Pledge Spark the Rally

On October 13, Meta Platforms released Muse Wonder, its first frontier AI model. Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg also publicly defended Meta Platforms' AI capital spending, committing to continue it at scale. Together, the launch and the pledge signal that Meta Platforms plans to compete at the leading edge of AI without easing off the outlays behind that push.

Advertising revenue funds Meta Platforms' AI spending. That equation leans entirely on ads, so the model's value to Meta Platforms runs through engagement and ad pricing. A model that increases engagement and supports higher ad prices is the path to a return on the investment.

The five most valuable companies in the world are U.S. stocks Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon. And 16 of the world's top 20 most valuable companies are U.S. firms.

The sheer size of these companies makes the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), Nasdaq-100, and index funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) linked to these benchmarks increasingly top-heavy. Meaning that just a handful of stocks and themes can drive performance, for better or worse.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Concentration is amplified for investors with dual exposure to these massive companies through ETFs and their individual holdings. The focused structure has paid off big time for U.S. investors -- as U.S. stocks have generally outperformed international stocks since the financial crisis of 2008.

However, some investors may be looking to diversify their portfolios by investing in leading international companies such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM), Samsung Electronics (OTC: SSNLF), SK Hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY), and ASML (NASDAQ: ASML).

You won't find these stocks in S&P 500 index funds because they aren't U.S.-based. You also won't find them in many popular growth ETFs, like the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF, which is benchmarked to a U.S.-specific index called the Morningstar U.S. Large Cap Growth Index.

Investors looking for an ETF built around international stocks have come to the right place. Here's why the Vanguard Total International Stock ETF (NASDAQ: VXUS) may be worth a closer look in October.

Image source: Getty Images.
8,790 international stock holdings

The Vanguard Total International Stock ETF holds 8,790 stocks from around the world. Japan makes up 15.5% of the fund, followed by 8.7% of companies in Taiwan, 8.3% UK companies, 8.1% Canada, 7% China, 6.4% South Korea, 5% France, 5% Switzerland, 4.8% Gemmany 4.4%, India, 4.3% Australia, and 22.5% other.

So compared to the S&P 500, where a single stock like Nvidia makes up 8.1% of the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO), entire countries have similar weights in the Total International Stock ETF.

The Total International Stock ETF is far more diversified. The world's largest semiconductor foundry operator -- Taiwan Semiconductor -- semiconductor designers and manufacturers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix -- and semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML are the four largest holdings. But they account for only 8.7% of the ETF. Beyond that, each holding accounts for less than 1% of the fund because only three non-U.S. stocks (excluding Saudi Arabian Oil, which the ETF doesn't own) have market caps over $1 trillion. For comparison, the four largest holdings in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF make up 26.2% of the ETF.

title: Microsoft’s Azure Grew 40% and Is Still Reportedly Hunting for 20% Cost Cuts
detail:
Microsoft’s Azure Grew 40% and Is Still Reportedly Hunting for 20% Cost Cuts

Azure grew 40% to $102B in revenue, but Microsoft's surging capex bill is driving reported demands for 20% cost cuts inside the unit.

Alphabet's Google Cloud has outpaced Azure with growth ranging from 32% to 63%, and both companies report earnings on October 28.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Microsoft didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat MSFT. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Azure group at Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) was told to cut costs by at least 20%, and Microsoft denied it the same day. The stock closed down 1.80% at $533.69. That left a $3.96 trillion market value, back below $4 trillion after a $4.04 trillion close on October 13.

Gorodenkoff / Shutterstock.com
MSFT Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

The report, which cited people familiar with the plans, said Girish Bablani, head of the Azure group that builds software for Microsoft's cloud servers, asked team leaders for the cuts. That group has about 11,500 staff.

Azure brought in $101.9 billion in revenue in the 12 months ending in June, up 40% from a year earlier. A business growing that fast seldom goes looking for a fifth of its cost base unless the growth costs more than it appears to or the money is needed for something bigger, and at Microsoft both may be true.

Reported Target Versus Company Denial

The reported savings would help pay for AI data center spending and for higher pay to keep engineers that rivals such as Anthropic are trying to hire. Ending contracts with outside vendors was one possible step.

The report did not say whether it would cut jobs. A spokesperson said "Azure leadership has not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans," and added, "Every responsible company prepares for a range of scenarios and market dynamics, both positive and negative."

Cutting costs inside Azure is the most direct way to hold that margin while the capex bill keeps climbing.

Anthropic's 50% quarterly revenue growth could push its 2027 revenue past $100 billion, with an IPO valuation potentially reaching $2 trillion.

Microsoft's stock gained just 4% versus the S&P 500's 16% as its legacy business drags valuation and AI revenue is never broken out separately.

Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon face the same legacy revenue trap, putting investor returns at risk without sustained mid-double-digit growth.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now, and Microsoft didn't make the cut. Enter your email to see the names that beat MSFT. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

Yesterday, Anthropic announced that its revenue grew 50% quarter over quarter to $16.8 billion. On the back of an envelope, its 2027 revenue could exceed $100 billion. That is about Morgan Stanley's annual revenue. However, Anthropic's top line could still be rising in the high double digits, just as Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) is today.

With that growth and its position at the center of the AI sector, Anthropic's IPO valuation could reach a staggering $2 trillion.

Microsoft via YouTube

Anthropic's revenue, revenue growth, and valuation are a real challenge to the stock prices and market caps of publicly traded companies whose shares are largely based on their AI businesses. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) is a prime example. Its market cap is $3.9 trillion. But its shares have lagged the market badly over the last year. They are up only 4%, while the S&P 500 is higher by 16%.

Microsoft has a huge drag. That is its legacy business, which will be bigger than its AI-based operations for the next several quarters, or much longer. This is a boat anchor for valuation.

Microsoft's financials are nothing special compared to most other huge public tech companies. In its most recent quarter, revenue was $90 billion, but that was up (only) 18%. Diluted EPS was up 32% to $4.81. The first full paragraph of the earnings release mentioned Xbox.

UBS raised its target to $675 from $525, citing Azure and Microsoft 365 fundamentals despite higher growth expectations.

Citi analyst Tyler Radke raised the firm's price target to $636 from $600 and maintained a 'Buy' rating.

UMass Memorial Health partnered with Microsoft and Accenture on a multi-year Azure data-platform initiative that will connect clinical, operational and research data and introduce AI tools to automate workflows.

Microsoft (MSFT) is drawing fresh analyst attention on Thursday ahead of its upcoming earnings report, with four firms raising their price targets on the stock.

According to The Fly, TD Cowen, Mizuho, Citi and UBS raised their Microsoft price targets, citing Azure trends, cloud demand and enterprise AI adoption.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

MSFT stock traded nearly 0.5% higher at the time of writing.

Analysts Highlight Cloud Demand And AI Spending

According to The Fly, TD Cowen raised its price target on Microsoft to $625 from $540 and maintained a 'Buy' rating. The firm updated its model ahead of quarterly results, seeing the potential for a "higher than normal" beat on Azure as the third-party data it tracks screened strongest in history, alongside a full quarter of Fairwater and a bullish read on an OpenAI growth inflection.

Mizuho analyst Gregg Moskowitz raised the firm's price target to $600 from $510 and maintained an 'Outperform' rating. Moskowitz said Mizuho's channel checks in Q3 were "very healthy overall," with strong public cloud and consumption data points and AI adoption remaining robust.

Citi analyst Tyler Radke raised the firm's price target to $636 from $600 and maintained a 'Buy' rating, according to The Fly. Citi said its recent chief investment officer survey and reseller checks reinforced its view that Microsoft's core productivity and public cloud franchise should accelerate as enterprises increase AI spending. The analyst also considers Microsoft among the best-positioned AI vendors.

Meanwhile, UBS analyst Karl Keirstead raised the price target on the stock to $675 from $525 and maintained a 'Buy' rating. He said the stock's 39% rally had raised growth expectations, but Azure and Microsoft 365 fundamentals supported the optimism and the valuation remained reasonable.

Microsoft Expands Healthcare AI Initiative

Separately, UMass Memorial Health announced a multi-year initiative with Microsoft and Accenture (ACN) to modernize its data platform using Microsoft Azure. The unified platform is intended to replace siloed reporting systems and support more advanced analytics.
